analysis.one_liner: Reinstates lapsed taxes on petroleum and chemical companies to fund toxic waste cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 24 cosponsors including one Republican, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund is the government program that cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. Until 1995, it was paid for by fees on the petroleum and chemical companies whose pollution created these sites; when those fees expired, the cleanup bill shifted to general taxpayers. This bill would have reinstated the polluter fees — the per-barrel petroleum tax and a corporate environmental income tax — through 2014, putting cleanup costs back on the companies responsible.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who have been paying for toxic waste cleanups out of general revenues since the industry fees lapsed in 1995, and communities living near contaminated sites, who would benefit from a restored cleanup fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate — an excise tax on petroleum — through January 1, 2014, so the cleanup fund is replenished by industry rather than general tax revenue.
Reinstates the Corporate Environmental Income Tax through January 1, 2014, taxing corporate income at an environmental rate dedicated to Superfund financing.
Removes an exemption that allowed crude oil exported from the United States to escape the per-barrel excise tax, tightening the tax so more oil is covered.

analysis.who_pays: Petroleum and chemical companies, which would again pay per-barrel excise taxes and the corporate environmental income tax — the same financing that funded the program from 1986 to 1995.

drawbacks.text: The excise taxes are partly passed through to consumers, so the price of petroleum products and chemicals would rise somewhat, spreading some of the cost beyond the polluting companies themselves.

The corporate environmental income tax applies to all corporations, not just the companies responsible for toxic sites, so some firms with no link to Superfund waste would pay for cleanups they did not cause.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill restores the 'polluter pays' arrangement that funded Superfund cleanups from 1986 to 1995. The main costs are modest price increases passed to consumers and taxation of corporations unconnected to the sites being cleaned. The design follows the original statutory scheme, so it is not badly targeted, but it is a blunt instrument compared with assessing only the companies that actually created the waste.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on January 15, 2003, joined by five original cosponsors including Republican Lincoln Chafee and Independent Jim Jeffords.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
It drew 24 cosponsors in total: 22 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent.
No further action was taken; the bill never left the Finance Committee and expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petroleum and chemical companies, which avoided paying the reinstated excise and corporate environmental taxes, and general taxpayers did not get relief — the cleanup burden stayed on ordinary taxpayers rather than returning to industry.

for.name: Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the Superfund polluter-pays taxes and led the push for cosponsors.

for.name: Lincoln Chafee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: 22 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Joe Biden, Dick Durbin, and Jon Corzine.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 15, 2003 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Charles Grassley
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup for the bill, keeping it from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: All but two of the 24 cosponsors were Democrats — 22 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent — and no roll-call votes were ever taken on the bill.

industries.note: The bill reinstates the per-barrel Hazardous Substance Superfund excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products, which they have not paid since 1995, and removes an export exemption. Their cleanup-fund contribution shifts back onto them; if the tax is passed through, consumers pay part of it.

The corporate environmental income tax and the Superfund financing regime fall on the chemical industry whose waste created many of the toxic sites, and whose fees funded cleanup until they expired. Its expiration has left cleanup costs with general taxpayers.

The reinstated corporate environmental income tax applies broadly to corporate taxable income, not only to companies linked to hazardous waste, so many firms would pay toward cleanups they had no role in creating.
